lead: Four quantities decide how well an antenna turns power into a wave and back. Radiation resistance turns radiated power into an equivalent resistor; radiation efficiency says what fraction of the input escapes instead of heating the metal; effective aperture says how much of an incoming wave is captured; polarization says whether wave and antenna agree on the direction of the electric field.
prereq: You need: directivity and gain from antenna parameters, and Prad of the Hertzian dipole.

blocks.text: A driven antenna draws current as if a resistor sat at its terminals, though the power has really left as a wave. The radiation resistance Rr is that resistor:
Prad = ½ |I|² Rr. Prad in W; I is the peak current in A at a stated point (the terminals or the current maximum); Rr in Ω. With an rms current the ½ goes
The reference point matters because the current varies along an antenna. A half-wave dipole has 73 Ω at its feed, which is its current maximum; a quarter-wave monopole has 36.5 Ω.

Short dipoles have two conventions. With the same current all along (the Hertzian dipole), Rr = 80π²(l/λ)². A real centre-fed short dipole has a current falling linearly to zero at the tips; its average current is half the feed current, its field half as strong, so referred to the feed Rr = 20π²(l/λ)². On this triangular convention Rr is 1.97 Ω at l = λ/10, 0.49 Ω at λ/20 and only 0.079 Ω at λ/50. The square law holds only for short dipoles; by l = λ/2 the current is a cosine and Rr is 73 Ω.

Metal resistance (raised by the skin effect as √f), dielectric loss and any loading coil are lumped into a loss resistance RL in series with Rr, so ZA = Rr + RL + jXA. The same current flows through both, so power divides in proportion to them.
ηrad = Rr / (Rr + RL). ηrad is the radiation efficiency, a ratio from 0 to 1

Gain follows as G = η<sub>rad</sub> D. Small antennas are hard to make efficient because R<sub>r</sub> is small. With R<sub>L</sub> = 0.5 Ω, a λ/10 dipole (1.97 Ω) has η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.80, a λ/20 dipole 0.50, and a λ/50 dipole only 0.079/0.579 = 0.14: 86 per cent of its input power heats the wire and coil. A half-wave dipole at 73 Ω sits far above any normal loss and is naturally efficient.
A DC ohmmeter cannot measure R<sub>r</sub>; it exists only at the working frequency, as power that leaves.

On receive, an antenna acts as a catching area. If a wave of power density S (W/m²) makes the antenna, matched in polarization and impedance, deliver Pr watts, the effective aperture is Ae = Pr/S in m². It is tied to directivity:
Aem = D λ² / 4π. Aem is the maximum effective aperture of a lossless antenna in m²; with loss, Ae = ηrad Aem = G λ²/4π

Ae is not the metal’s area. A half-wave dipole at 300 MHz (λ = 1 m) is a thin wire 0.5 m long, yet Ae = 1.64 × 1²/4π = 0.131 m². The relation is derived in the chapter on receiving antennas. For horns and dishes the aperture efficiency eap = Ae/Aphys stays below 1 because the field across the mouth is not uniform and some power spills past the rim; dishes reach 0.5 to 0.7, giving the dish gain G = eap(πd/λ)² for diameter d.

sections.h3: Polarization and the polarization loss factor

blocks.text: The polarization of a wave is the path traced by the tip of its electric field at a fixed point, seen as the wave approaches. Linear: a straight line. Circular: a circle, when two equal perpendicular components are 90° apart in time; the sense of rotation gives right-hand or left-hand circular. Elliptical: the general case. The axial ratio AR, major axis over minor axis of the ellipse, is 1 for circular and infinite for linear. An antenna’s polarization is that of the wave it radiates.

Two crossed dipoles fed with equal currents 90° apart radiate circular polarization along their common broadside; fed in phase they radiate linear polarization at 45°. A receiving antenna picks up only the part of the field that matches its own polarization:

PLF = |ρ̂w · ρ̂a|² = cos²ψp. ρ̂w and ρ̂a are the unit polarization vectors of the wave and of the antenna; ψp is the angle between two linear polarizations; PLF is a ratio from 0 to 1 that multiplies the received power

figure.caption: Radiation efficiency of a centre-fed short dipole, computed from R<sub>r</sub> = 20π²(l/λ)². With the worked example’s 0.5 Ω of loss, a λ/20 dipole radiates only half its input, a λ/50 dipole 14 per cent; cutting the loss to 0.1 Ω lifts the whole curve.

spec.aria: Plot of radiation efficiency from 0 to 1 against dipole length from 0 to 0.12 wavelengths, for loss resistances of 0.5 and 0.1 ohm. On the 0.5 ohm curve the points lambda over 50 at 0.14, lambda over 20 at 0.50 and lambda over 10 at 0.80 are marked.

examples.question: A centre-fed short dipole is λ/20 long and has a loss resistance R<sub>L</sub> = 0.5 Ω. Find (a) its radiation resistance with the triangular current, (b) its radiation efficiency and gain in dBi (D = 1.5), and (c) its effective aperture at 300 MHz with and without the loss.
steps: R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub> = 0.493 + 0.5 = 0.993 Ω, so η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.493/0.993 = 0.497, about 50 per cent.
G = η<sub>rad</sub> D = 0.497 × 1.5 = 0.745, that is 10 log₁₀ 0.745 = −1.28 dBi: the loss more than cancels the 1.76 dBi of directivity.
λ = c/f = 3 × 10⁸/(300 × 10⁶) = 1 m (so the dipole is 5 cm long).
With loss: A<sub>e</sub> = η<sub>rad</sub> A<sub>em</sub> = 0.497 × 0.119 = 0.0593 m².
examples.answer: R<sub>r</sub> = 0.493 Ω; η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.497; G = 0.745 (−1.28 dBi); A<sub>em</sub> = 0.119 m², falling to 0.0593 m² with the loss.

examples.question: A wave of power density S = 1 mW/m² reaches an antenna whose effective aperture is 0.02 m². Find the received power when (a) both are vertically polarized, (b) the antenna is tilted 30° from the wave’s linear polarization, (c) the wave is circular and the antenna linear, (d) the antenna is horizontal.
steps: Matched power: S A<sub>e</sub> = 10⁻³ × 0.02 = 2 × 10⁻⁵ W = 20 µW.
(b) PLF = cos²30° = 0.75: P<sub>r</sub> = 15 µW, a loss of 10 log₁₀(1/0.75) = 1.25 dB.
(c) A circular wave has equal components along any two perpendicular lines; the linear antenna takes one of them, PLF = 0.5: P<sub>r</sub> = 10 µW, a 3.01 dB loss.
(d) Vertical wave, horizontal antenna: PLF = cos²90° = 0, so P<sub>r</sub> = 0 in theory; in practice a cross-polar null is 20 to 30 dB down, not zero.

traps: Quoting R<sub>r</sub> without the reference point or the current convention. 80π²(l/λ)² is uniform current; 20π²(l/λ)² is a centre-fed short dipole referred to its feed current.
Using A<sub>e</sub> = λ²/4π for every antenna. That is the isotropic value (D = 1); multiply by D, or by G if loss is counted.

Mixing peak and rms current in P<sub>rad</sub> = ½|I|²R<sub>r</sub>. This doubles or halves R<sub>r</sub>; the resulting efficiency error depends on R<sub>L</sub>, so it is not a simple factor of two.
Assuming a resonant antenna is efficient. Resonance only cancels the reactance; efficiency is set by R<sub>r</sub> against R<sub>L</sub>.
Calling AR = 1 linear. AR = 1 is circular; a linear wave has AR → ∞, and a linear antenna receiving a circular wave loses 3 dB.

quiz.q: Define radiation resistance and state what must be specified with it.
quiz.a: The resistance R<sub>r</sub> for which ½|I|²R<sub>r</sub> equals the radiated power. The point where I is taken (terminals or current maximum) must be stated.

quiz.q: Give R<sub>r</sub> of a half-wave dipole and of a quarter-wave monopole, and the reason for the ratio.
quiz.a: 73 Ω and 36.5 Ω. The monopole and its image form a dipole, but only the half above the ground plane radiates, so the same current gives half the power.

quiz.q: Why does a very short dipole have poor efficiency even with small loss?
quiz.a: R<sub>r</sub> falls as (l/λ)², to 0.079 Ω at λ/50. With 0.5 Ω of loss, η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.079/0.579 = 0.14, so most of the power heats the wire and coil.

quiz.q: An antenna has D = 20 and η<sub>rad</sub> = 0.9 at 3 GHz. Find its gain in dBi and its effective aperture.
A dish 0.6 m across works at 12 GHz with aperture efficiency 0.6. Find its gain in dBi.
Two crossed dipoles are fed with equal currents. What polarization results at 90° feed phase difference, and at 0°?
quiz.a: At 90° the two perpendicular fields are equal and in time quadrature, so the resultant rotates: circular, with the sense set by the sign of the 90°. At 0° they add on one line at 45°: linear, AR = ∞.

beyond: Not for the exam. Small antennas in phones and IoT sensors run into the Chu limit, which ties bandwidth to size in wavelengths; satellite and 5G links use dual-polarized antennas for polarization diversity and MIMO. Search next for “Chu limit” and “polarization diversity”.
